title: Sony Music moves to add more than 30,000 copyrighted recordings to its lawsuit against Udio

reading.body:
The core failure here is training a generative AI system on copyrighted material without obtaining licenses from the rights holders. Udio's model learned to produce music from a corpus that allegedly included protected recordings, and the outputs were close enough to existing works, such as The Temptations' "My Girl," that major labels pursued legal action. The failure occurred at the data-collection and model-training stage, well before any user ever typed a text prompt. A licensing review of training data before deployment would have been the point at which this could have been caught.

The legal picture is still unresolved in several directions. Sony filed a separate lawsuit alleging the training corpus included more than 30,000 recordings, a court declined to add those recordings to the original case, and a class action by independent artists survived a dismissal attempt and was transferred to New York. A musicians' union also sued over UMG's settlement deal itself. None of these cases has produced a final verdict, and the allegations of copying are not yet findings of fact.

What is established is that two of the three major labels reached settlements with Udio and moved toward licensing arrangements, while the third escalated. The settlement terms are not public, and the compensation structure for artists who opt into the new licensed platform has not been disclosed. Whether the eventual licensed platform resolves the underlying copyright questions, or simply sidesteps them commercially, is not yet determined.

summary:
Universal Music Group has settled a lawsuit against AI music startup Udio, which had been accused of using copyrighted songs to train its artificial intelligence model. The dispute centered on allegations that Udio created music similar to existing hits, such as The Temptations' "My Girl," without permission or compensation. Under the new licensing agreements, Udio will launch a platform next year trained exclusively on authorized and licensed music, allowing users to customize, stream, and share songs they create. Financial terms of the settlement were not disclosed.

This settlement marks Udio's first licensing agreement with a major record label and reflects the growing tensions between entertainment companies and AI startups over copyright protection. Udio, founded in 2024 by former Google DeepMind employees, lets users generate original songs from text prompts. The company said artists can opt into the new platform and will receive compensation, though specific details remain undisclosed. UMG also announced a separate partnership with Stability AI to develop music creation tools for artists and producers.
